SENTINEL-RAT · Heidelberg Zoo

Photograph or heat — drag between them

Every capture from this enclosure is two pictures taken together: an ordinary photograph, and a map of how warm each surface is. Drag the slider to fade from one to the other. Nine real captures, from before dawn to after dusk.

Nine captures

When the surroundings are cool, an animal stands out as heat. Once bedding has been sitting in the sun, that difference collapses — and in one capture here it reverses, with the animal reading colder than the ground it is sitting on.

What the two toggles do

Sensor grid swaps the smooth heat map for what the sensor actually measured: a grid of 80 × 62 readings, about 5,000 numbers for the whole scene. The smooth version is that same data, interpolated. It is worth seeing once, because it explains why heat can tell you something is there and not what it is.

Show boxes draws the outlines a person drew by hand around each animal, looking at both pictures. They are not the output of any detector — they are the ground truth a detector would be trained on.

The black border that appears as you fade towards heat is real: the heat camera sees a narrower slice of the scene than the photograph does.
